title: Stateless Design Principles
description: Understand what stateless design means, why it matters for scalability, and how to implement it correctly across services.

data.text: Stateless design means a service does not store client state between requests. Every request contains all the information needed to process it. This property is fundamental to horizontal scaling because any instance can serve any request without needing prior knowledge.

If services store state in memory, adding new servers breaks routing. A user's session might live on server A, but the load balancer routes the next request to server B. Stateless services eliminate this coupling, making load balancing, failover, and auto-scaling reliable.

items: Simpler load balancing—any instance can handle any request
Easy failover: if one instance dies, traffic shifts seamlessly
Auto-scaling works predictably without sticky-session complexity
Deployments and rollbacks are safer because instances are interchangeable
Testing is easier since each request is self-contained

data.title: Rule of Thumb
data.text: Push state out of the service tier. Store it in databases, caches, object storage, or dedicated session stores so the application layer remains stateless.

data.caption: Stateless services backed by shared external state stores
data.definition:
flowchart TD
    Client --> LB[Load Balancer]
    LB --> S1[Service 1]
    LB --> S2[Service 2]
    LB --> S3[Service 3]
    S1 & S2 & S3 --> DB[(Database)]
    S1 & S2 & S3 --> Cache[(Redis / Cache)]
    S1 & S2 & S3 --> Queue[(Message Queue)]

items.question: Can stateless services have local caches?
items.answer: Yes. Local caches can improve performance as long as the service behaves correctly if the cache is empty or stale. The cache is an optimization, not a source of truth.

items.question: Are JWT tokens stateless?
items.answer: Yes. JWTs encode session data in the token itself, so no server-side session storage is needed. However, revocation requires extra mechanisms such as blocklists or short expiration windows.

items.question: Does stateless mean no state anywhere?
items.answer: No. It means the service tier does not hold request-specific state. Databases, caches, and message queues can and should still maintain state.

data.title: Summary
points: Stateless services can handle any request at any time.
Push state to dedicated external stores.
Local caches are acceptable as read-through optimizations.
Stateless design unlocks auto-scaling and resilient deployments.
data.takeaway: If your service cannot be restarted without losing user context, it is not truly stateless.
